curation.lead:
Jackie Fine Arts Inc was a Pennsylvania-incorporated entity controlled by Herman Finesod through M and J Holding Corporation. Beginning in the early 1980s, the company acquired reproduction rights to works by Picasso and other artists — purchased through intermediary AMI from Paraselenes SA, a Marina Picasso company — at a cost of approximately $10,000 per master. It then sold those rights to more than 2,000 investors at prices between $225,000 and $250,000 each, supported by fraudulent independent appraisals valuing each master at $700,000–$750,000 [Finding #2131]. By 1986 the company carried $409 million in notes receivable from buyers, and M and J Holding's 1986 tax return reported total assets of $1.33 billion [Finding #2117]. The scheme's core was the tax deduction: investors were told they could deduct the appraised value rather than the purchase price.

The appraisal infrastructure underpinning the scheme was itself fraudulent. Sigmund Rothschild charged $250 per appraisal; F. Peter Rose charged $150–$300 each and paid Rothschild a $50 kickback per transaction. The two appraisers shared an office and a secretary — a conflict never disclosed to investors — and together produced approximately 2,500 appraisals [Finding #2131]. An unnamed Los Angeles law firm provided tax opinions while secretly receiving one percent of cash proceeds from each sale [Finding #2131]. The IRS disallowed all resulting deductions; the Sixth Circuit affirmed in Rose v. Commissioner, 868 F.2d 851 (6th Cir. 1989), holding that the art master packages lacked economic substance and that investors had no honest profit motive [Finding #2135].

Civil litigation followed across at least twelve federal and state courts in more than ten jurisdictions from 1983 through 1992 [Finding #2139]. The bellwether case, Faircloth v. Finesod, 938 F.2d 513 (4th Cir. 1991), resulted in jury findings of fraud, RICO violations, and civil conspiracy, with punitive damages of $5 million against Jackie Fine Arts, $2.5 million against Finesod personally, and $500,000 against Rose, plus over $615,000 in attorney fees [Finding #2130]. Finesod filed personal bankruptcy in the Western District of Pennsylvania in 1994 [Finding #2106]. A German subsidiary, Jackie Fine Arts GmbH (Handelsregister HRB 58801, Munich), was separately registered and has since been removed [Finding #2136]. Bernard Indyke — father of Jeffrey Epstein's longtime attorney Darren Indyke — served as manager and board member of the company during this period; Jackie Fine Arts was a client of the law firm Gold and Wachtel [Finding #2099].
curation.system_role: Jackie Fine Arts Inc was a tax shelter operation controlled by Herman Finesod that sold overvalued art reproduction rights to investors, generating over $409 million in notes receivable before collapsing under IRS disallowance and nationwide civil litigation. Its significance to the broader investigation derives from Bernard Indyke's board role and the company's status as a Gold and Wachtel client, which placed it on a direct institutional line to Jeffrey Epstein.

sections.title: Financial Activity
sections.content:
Jackie Fine Arts acquired Picasso reproduction rights from Paraselenes SA — a company controlled by Marina Picasso — through an intermediary identified as AMI, at a cost of roughly $10,000 per master [Finding #2131]. Those rights were resold to investors at $225,000–$250,000 each, a markup of 22 to 25 times cost [Finding #2117]. By 1986 the company held $409 million in notes receivable, and its parent, M and J Holding Corporation, reported total assets of $1.33 billion on its 1986 tax return [Finding #2117]. Approximately 2,000 investors participated; total appraisals numbered around 2,500 [Finding #2131].

The appraisal chain was structurally corrupted at inception. Rothschild and Rose — who shared office space and administrative staff — produced valuations of $700,000–$750,000 per master against a $10,000 cost basis, while Rothschild received a $50 kickback on each Rose appraisal [Finding #2131]. An unnamed Los Angeles law firm that provided tax shelter opinions to investors simultaneously received one percent of cash sales — a conflict undisclosed to the investors relying on those opinions [Finding #2131]. The IRS ultimately disallowed all claimed deductions, and the Sixth Circuit held in Rose v. Commissioner, 868 F.2d 851 (1989), that the packages lacked economic substance [Finding #2135].

The connection to the broader network: Bernard Indyke served as manager and board member of Jackie Fine Arts during its operating years. Gold and Wachtel represented the company as a client. It was through this firm that Bernard's son, Darren Indyke, later joined as an associate, eventually becoming Jeffrey Epstein's primary attorney [Finding #2099].

sections.title: Legal Proceedings
sections.content:
Federal civil litigation against Jackie Fine Arts and Herman Finesod began in 1983 and continued through 1992 across at least twelve courts [Finding #2139]. Documented cases include: Turner v. JFA (S.D. Cal. 1983), Menish v. JFA (C.D. Cal. 1984), Ross v. JFA (D.S.C. 1985), Westheimer v. Finesod (S.D. Tex. 1986), Nichols v. JFA (D. Me. 1987), Bergin v. JFA (D. Minn. 1987), Faircloth v. JFA (E.D.N.Y. and S.D. Fla. 1989), Ross v. JFA (S.D. Cal. 1990–1992), and Burch v. JFA (E.D.N.Y. 1992) [Finding #2106]. State court proceedings arose in Arizona, Wyoming, and Alabama [Finding #2139]. A multi-district securities matter, Terra-Drill Partnerships Securities Litigation (MDL No. 791), was separately identified as a Finesod vehicle [Finding #2139].

The dispositive civil case was Faircloth v. Finesod, 938 F.2d 513 (4th Cir. 1991). A jury found Jackie Fine Arts liable for fraud, civil RICO violations, and civil conspiracy. Punitive damages totaled $5 million against Jackie Fine Arts, $2.5 million against Finesod personally, and $500,000 against appraiser Rose, with attorney fees of over $615,000 [Finding #2130]. Finesod also faced personal suits including Vigil v. Finesod (D.N.M. 1987), Levi v. Finesod (S.D.N.Y. 1992), and filed personal bankruptcy in the Western District of Pennsylvania in 1994 [Finding #2106].

On the tax side, the IRS disallowed all deductions claimed through the art master packages. The Sixth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court in Rose v. Commissioner, 868 F.2d 851 (1989), ruling that the packages lacked economic substance and that participating investors had no honest profit motive [Finding #2135].

sections.title: Corporate Structure and Key Personnel
sections.content:
Jackie Fine Arts Inc was wholly owned by M and J Holding Corporation, which was in turn owned by Herman Finesod [Finding #2117]. Bernard Indyke served as manager and member of the board; the company was a client of Gold and Wachtel, the New York law firm [Finding #2099]. A German subsidiary, Jackie Fine Arts GmbH, was registered in Munich (Handelsregister HRB 58801) and has since been struck from the register, indicating the company had international operations beyond its U.S. base [Finding #2136]. The U.S. entity has not been found in active corporate registries, consistent with its dissolution following litigation and Finesod's 1994 bankruptcy.

The relevance to the Epstein network flows through personnel rather than direct financial overlap: Bernard Indyke's role at Jackie Fine Arts placed him and Gold and Wachtel in the same institutional environment, which is where Darren Indyke began his legal career and first encountered Jeffrey Epstein as a client [Finding #2099].

What is the identity of the unnamed Los Angeles law firm that provided tax opinions while receiving one percent of cash sales, and did that firm have any subsequent connection to Epstein or Finesod?
Did Bernard Indyke receive any compensation, legal fees, or other benefit from Jackie Fine Arts that was recorded in the litigation record?
Are there corporate registry records in any U.S. state identifying the precise period of Bernard Indyke's tenure as manager and board member, and any other named officers or directors?
What was the disposition of the $409 million in notes receivable — were any investors made whole in the bankruptcy proceedings, and how were the proceeds tracked?
